transcript:
Header: 2027-04-06 15:00 UTC | Duration: 48m | Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Jordan (Redwood SE), Priya (Argos Platform Eng), Carlos (Argos Data Eng), Ellen (Argos ML Ops)

Summary: Quick scoping to convert Argos' latency targets to TTFT/TPOT SLOs, agree on p95/p99 targets, outline measurement cadence and traffic sampling for the pilot benchmark. Discussed traffic shaping, variable payloads (short prompts vs long context), and security controls for a dedicated pilot environment.

Topics: SLO definitions, TTFT vs TPOT tradeoffs, p95/p99 targets, traffic profile & payload sampling, benchmark harness plan, dedicated vs hosted routing for pilot, security/compliance handoffs.

--- Transcript ---
00:00 Maya (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call and then Jordan will jump into the measurement plan. Priya, Carlos, Ellen, can you hear us okay?
00:06 Priya (Argos): Yep, good here. Thanks Maya.
00:08 Ellen (Argos): Good, can hear you.
00:10 Carlos (Argos): yeah, thanks.
00:12 Jordan (Redwood SE): cool, I'll share screen in a sec but the goal today is narrow: convert your existing latency goals into explicit SLOs we can measure in the pilot, and agree on sampling and acceptance gating.
00:22 Priya: Great. Our product team says we need a median first-token below 300ms and tail below 1s for chat-ish flows, but they're open to tradeoffs if we show cost impact.
00:32 Maya: okay that's helpful. Quick question — when you say median first-token, is that measured from your frontend client to Redwood's API or from our runtime entry? We need to be explicit.
00:41 Priya: From client, yes. But we can give you edge-to-runtime deltas.
00:45 Jordan: Perfect. For pilot SLOs we recommend splitting into TTFT (time to first token) and TPOT (total per-token) metrics. TTFT captures latency-sensitive UX, TPOT ties to cost and throughput.
00:57 Carlos: been reading the docs — TTFT vs TPOT — can you remind the measurement difference?
01:02 Jordan: Sure. TTFT is the duration from request arrival at the serving entry point to the first model token emitted. TPOT is total time per token or per-response completion, often normalized as tokens/sec or per-token ms; for SLOs we use p95/p99 of TTFT and average TPOT under load.
01:18 Priya: We definitely care about p95 and p99 for TTFT. The product team will accept p95 320ms, p99 900ms for priority flows. Are those realistic?
01:28 Jordan: Those seem achievable on hosted with batching tuned, but they depend heavily on payload size distribution, sequence length, and KV cache hit rates. For 4k context models it's different than a short prompt.
01:38 Ellen: Our traffic is mixed — maybe 65% short prompts (under 150 tokens), 25% medium (150-800), and 10% long (800-2k). We can provide histograms.
01:49 Maya: That's excellent. That distribution will drive batching windows and kernel selection. For p99 targets we often separate measurement by traffic class — e.g., short vs long — otherwise p99 gets dominated by the long tails.
01:59 Carlos: So do we set a single p99 across all traffic or per-class?
02:03 Jordan: Recommend per-class SLOs for the pilot, then a weighted aggregate for acceptance. For example: short p95 250ms p99 650ms; medium p95 420ms p99 1.1s; long p95 1.2s p99 3.5s, then weighted TPOT budget overall.
02:18 Priya: Okay that sounds reasonable. How do you measure TTFT in the benchmark harness?
02:22 Jordan: We instrument at the load-generator and at the runtime ingress. Ideally we capture client-side timestamps, loadgen timestamps, and server ingress/egress to compute client-to-first-token and runtime-first-token. The harness will report p50/p95/p99 and show stall reasons (e.g., queuing, model kernel latency).
02:36 Maya: we'll send the harness and a spreadsheet that expects a 7-day histogram and sample payloads. The harness can replay with similar QPS profile and payload mix.
02:43 Priya: about throughput (TPOT), we care about sustained concurrency at 95% cost budget. Our finance team gave a notional monthly token cost target. How do you map TPOT to cost?
02:54 Jordan: TPOT correlates to tokens/sec and GPU utilization. We'll collect per-token time under steady load and compute tokens/sec per GPU; combine with pricing to get cost per 1M tokens. Also we'll propose batching thresholds to trade latency vs throughput for non-priority flows.
03:08 Carlos: For long responses, batching helps throughput but hurts TTFT, right?
03:12 Jordan: Exactly. That's the tradeoff. We support hybrid routing: latency-sensitive flows to a low-batch, low-latency pool; bulk flows to a high-batch pool. For the pilot we can do an initial split by route header.
03:24 Ellen: We have compliance constraints — pilot must run in a VPC and KMS for keys. Can Redwood support KMS integration?
03:29 Maya: Yes, Private + Dedicated support KMS. For the pilot we'll stand up a dedicated pool in your VPC. We'll provide the KMS integration guide in the security pack.
03:37 Priya: any special audit logs required?
03:39 Maya: We can enable full request/response logging with redaction and deliver audit logs to your S3 or Cloud Storage; we'll include retention settings. We'll send SOC2 artifacts too.
03:49 Priya: Great. Back to sampling — how many samples do you need to produce statistically significant p99?
03:54 Jordan: p99 needs a lot of samples. For a single p99 estimate with decent confidence you want thousands of samples; practically we run load windows with 10k+ requests per traffic class, or sample across multiple runs. That's why we ask for 7-day histograms to synthesize realistic burst patterns.
04:08 Carlos: Are we running both TTFT microbenchmarks and long-run sustained TPOT sweeps?
04:12 Jordan: Yes, standard plan is: (1) TTFT microbench for latency-sensitive routes with low concurrency, (2) TPOT sweeps ramping concurrency to map tokens/sec vs latency, (3) end-to-end replay with real traffic mix.
04:23 Priya: sounds good. On acceptance criteria, product wants canary-level pass: short and medium classes meet p95/p99 and aggregate TPOT cost within 15% of target. If not met, we have 1 optimization cycle.
04:36 Maya: We'll encode that in the pilot charter. Also include regression thresholds for quality — can't be just latency.
04:43 Ellen: Right — quality regressions are a blocker. We'll run a small eval set for coherence and hallucination rates.
04:49 Jordan: We'll integrate your eval set into the harness so latency runs are tied to quality checks; if quality drops we won't claim pass even if SLOs are met.
04:58 Priya: any red flags from your side?
05:00 Jordan: biggest risk is payload variance — if your production has sudden long-context bursts that the 7-day sample doesn't capture, p99 will vary. Cache warmup also matters — KV cache hits drastically reduce TTFT for follow-ups.
05:12 Carlos: About KV cache — our chat flow frequently references recent context. Can you show cache hit metrics?
05:17 Jordan: yes, runtime exposes per-request cache hit rate; harness can replay conversation-style sessions to estimate real-world cache benefits.
05:25 Maya: Operationally, we recommend a two-week pilot: week 1 install + warmup + small microbench; week 2 focused load tests and acceptance. Tentative windows: deploy week of 4/18, tests 4/25-4/29.
05:39 Priya: timeline works. Who owns config for routing rules?
05:43 Maya: Redwood will propose route config; Argos will review and we can iterate. For the pilot, Redwood will implement routing in the dedicated pool.
05:50 Carlos: for reporting, we need a dashboard with token-level cost, per-route p95/p99, and traces for outliers.
05:57 Jordan: Redwood Console provides those. We'll share a sample dashboard and link to logs.
06:02 Priya: pricing — will pilot be billable? Finance asked.
06:05 Maya: Pilot runs on reserved ephemeral capacity — there's a small refundable commitment to cover cost, we can share a quote.
06:11 Ellen: ok send quote.
06:13 Maya: Next steps recap: share benchmark harness and security pack (Maya), Argos export histograms + sample payloads (Priya), Jordan sends draft measurement plan and sampling table.
06:24 Priya: Thanks, that captures it. Couple minor clarifications — for p99, you recommended per-class thresholds. For acceptance we'll produce weighted aggregates and a pass/fail.
06:34 Jordan: yes exactly. We'll include the math in the measurement plan.
06:37 Maya: Anything else?
06:39 Carlos: One last Q — competitors. We did a cost run with InServe recently and their p95 was okay but p99 had lots of noise. Want to see how Redwood handles tails.
06:47 Jordan: We'll highlight tail smoothing and fallbacks in the plan — we have automatic routing fallback to smaller models if load spikes and the policy will be explicit.
06:55 Ellen: Great. Thanks everyone.
06:57 Maya: Thanks — we'll follow up by Friday with artifacts.
07:00 Meeting ends.

Notes on measurement plan (quick bullets):
- SLOs: TTFT per-class p95/p99; overall TPOT budget as tokens/sec and cost per 1M tokens.
- Sampling: Use 7-day histogram to synthesize traffic, run 3 separate load windows per class with 10k+ requests each to get stable p99 estimates.
- Benchmarks: 1) Microbench TTFT low concurrency (no batching), 2) TPOT ramp tests for throughput mapping, 3) End-to-end mixed-replay with real payload mix.
- Instrumentation: client, ingress, runtime-first-token, egress; collect KV cache hit rate, batch sizes, GPU util, per-token latency.
- Acceptance gating: per-class p95/p99 pass + aggregate TPOT cost within 15% of target + no quality regressions on eval set.
- Security: dedicated VPC pilot, KMS integration, audit logs delivered to Argos S3 with configurable retention.

Shared links mentioned during call:
- Benchmark harness repo: https://redwood.example.com/harness/argos-pilot (will be shared)
- Pilot spreadsheet template: https://redwood.example.com/pilots/argos-template.xlsx
- Security pack (SOC2/KMS): to be attached in follow-up email

End of transcript.
